analysis.one_liner: Abolishes eleven cabinet departments every ten years unless Congress votes to keep each one.
analysis.headline: The bill to abolish 11 cabinet departments was referred to the House Oversight Committee in April 2015 and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill flips the default for the federal government: eleven cabinet departments — Agriculture, Commerce, Education, Energy, Health and Human Services, Housing and Urban Development, Labor, Interior, the Treasury, Veterans Affairs, and Transportation — would be abolished on a schedule running from 2 to 11 years after passage, and every 10 years after that. Each one would survive only if both the House and Senate pass a resolution saying so; if they miss the deadline, the department disappears. The bill also sweeps in other agencies whose authorizing legislation went through certain committees, though it exempts the Defense, State, Homeland Security, and Justice departments.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the main beneficiaries would be advocates of sharply smaller federal government and lower federal spending, since eliminating these departments would end or scatter programs that together touch food safety, farm programs, Medicare and Medicaid administration, veterans' health care, workplace safety enforcement, student aid, housing assistance, and more. The bill's structure — agencies die unless Congress affirmatively saves them — is designed to make keeping government programs the exception rather than the rule.

how_it_helps.text: It would force Congress to affirmatively re-approve each of the eleven named departments, plus other agencies under specified House committees, at least once every 10 years, instead of programs continuing until Congress acts to change them.

Each agency scheduled for abolishment would have to report to Congress a year ahead, justifying its existence and identifying overlap with other agencies, which supporters present as an accountability review.

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on the affected departments would bear the cost: veterans served by the VA, seniors and low-income patients whose Medicare, Medicaid, and public health programs run through HHS, workers protected by Labor Department rules, farmers and food-safety programs under Agriculture, students receiving federal aid through Education, and low-income households receiving housing assistance through HUD. Federal employees in those departments would also lose their jobs if Congress failed to act.

drawbacks.text: The bill puts the Department of Veterans Affairs on the abolishment schedule, meaning veterans' health care and benefits administration would end unless both chambers of Congress passed a resolution to save the department within the deadline.

It also schedules the Departments of Health and Human Services, Labor, Agriculture, Education, Housing and Urban Development, and the Treasury for abolishment, which would end the administrative machinery for Medicare, Medicaid, workplace protections, food safety, student aid, housing assistance, and tax collection unless Congress re-approved each one.

The mechanism relies on Congress passing a concurrent resolution — a statement both chambers must agree on — for every agency on a fixed clock; a single missed deadline in either chamber abolishes the agency, with the bill providing only a one-year wind-down to dispose of assets and liabilities, not a plan for who takes over the agency's duties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — periodic review of whether agencies still justify their budgets — is a real idea, but this version achieves it by threatening to abolish the Departments of Veterans Affairs, Health and Human Services, Labor, Agriculture, and the Treasury outright if Congress misses a deadline. The wind-down process covers disposing of assets and liabilities but does not transfer ongoing responsibilities like veterans' care, Medicare administration, or tax collection to any successor. For most people, the risk of programs they depend on lapsing would outweigh the theoretical benefit of a sharper review process. The bill also conspicuously exempts the Defense, State, Homeland Security, and Justice departments, so the largest parts of the federal budget would not be subject to the same test.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Bradley Byrne (R-AL) introduced the bill on April 22, 2015, with 15 Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform the same day; the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action at any point afterward.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, with the bill still in committee, so it never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Anyone who relies on the affected departments — veterans, Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, workers, farmers, students, and federal employees in those agencies — is better off because the bill never advanced, since the services those departments deliver were never put at risk. No industry or interest group lost anything by the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on the departments' services

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Jason Chaffetz, R-UT, at the time)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — for the rest of the 114th Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Decides which bills reach the House floor
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 original supporters — the sponsor and 15 cosponsors — were Republicans, and the bill never drew a Democratic cosponsor or a floor vote.

industries.note: Eleven cabinet departments and a wide range of other agencies would be abolished on a fixed schedule unless Congress re-approved each one, ending the jobs and programs administered through them. Exemptions for Defense, State, Homeland Security, and Justice leave most of the security and defense establishment untouched.

The bill's default-abolish structure is designed to shrink the federal government's domestic footprint, which is this movement's central goal. The cost falls on people who receive services through the affected departments.

industries.industry: Federal program beneficiaries (veterans, seniors, students, farmers, low-income households)
industries.note: Their services — VA care, Medicare and Medicaid administration, student aid, farm programs, housing assistance — would lapse if Congress missed a re-approval deadline, since the bill provides only a one-year asset wind-down, not a transfer of duties to a successor.
